content.title: About
content.content: Lemon cupcake is a soft, fragrant cake with a bright citrus flavor, made from flour, sugar, eggs, butter, and fresh lemon juice and zest. It is often served as a dessert with tea or coffee and can also be used as a base for a layered cake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The lemon cupcake became popular in Europe in the 19th century as a light dessert for summer picnics.
The combination of lemon acidity and sweet batter creates a balanced taste that is enhanced by a powdered sugar glaze.
Traditionally the cupcake is baked in a “English” (English muffin) shape, but modern recipes use muffin or cupcake tins.
Lemon juice in the batter activates the leavening agents, making the cake more airy.
In some countries the lemon cupcake is decorated with lemon zest or finely chopped berries for a flavor contrast.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Lemons are rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and has antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low Fat Content
items.content: Compared with many sweet pastries, a lemon cupcake typically contains a moderate amount of butter, making it less fatty.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour in the recipe adds dietary fiber, which aids digestion.

items.title: Energy Boost
items.content: The mix of carbohydrates and a modest amount of protein provides a quick source of energy.

items.title: Mood Enhancement
items.content: Lemon aroma is known for its refreshing and calming effect, which can improve mood.

items.title: Citrus Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lemons, such as skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity of lemon juice can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Cupcakes often contain a notable amount of sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gluten Content
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making the cupcake unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lemon cupcake can be served as a standalone dessert, sliced into bite‑size pieces and topped with powdered sugar glaze, buttercream, or fresh berries. It is also convenient to take on the go as a quick snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cupcake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, keep it in the refrigerator – it will stay fresh for about a week. Bring the cupcake to room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Lentils are an annual legume cultivated for its edible seeds. Originating from the Mediterranean and Western Asia, they are now grown worldwide. Lentils have a mild, slightly earthy flavor, a firm yet tender texture, and come in several colors: green, brown, red, and black.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils belong to the Fabaceae family and are among the oldest cultivated crops – they were grown in ancient Egypt.
More than 50 lentil varieties exist, differing in color, size, and maturation time.
Red lentils cook the fastest – they are ready in 15‑20 minutes.
Lentils are protein‑rich, making them a popular meat substitute in vegetarian and vegan diets.
Global lentil production exceeded 5 million tonnes in the 2020s.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of cooked lentils provides about 9 g of protein, offering a valuable amino acid profile for plant‑based nutrition.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Lentils contain roughly 8 g of fiber per 100 g, supporting healthy digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The slow release of carbohydrates helps stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in iron and folate
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport, while folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lentils provide polyphenols and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to lentils, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of minerals such as iron and zinc. Soaking and sprouting lower its level.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Legumes, including lentils, can cause increased gas in sensitive individuals. Gradual introduction helps the digestive system adapt.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: People with gout are advised to limit lentil intake due to its moderate purine levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lentils can be boiled, stewed, added to soups, salads, stews, and veggie patties. They are also used to make purees, lentil flour for baking, and as a meat‑like filler in dishes. Soaking for 2‑4 hours speeds cooking and improves digestibility.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry lentils in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, they keep for 2‑3 years. Cooked lentils should be refrigerated and consumed within 4‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned pineapple in a juice pack (4024) consists of bite‑size pieces of ripe pineapple sealed in a hermetic pouch with its own juice. The product retains the bright aroma, sweet‑tart flavor, and most of the vitamins found in fresh pineapple.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pineapple is one of the few fruits that contain bromelain – an enzyme that aids protein digestion.
Packaging in its own juice preserves up to 80 % of vitamin C compared with products processed in syrup.
Native to South America, pineapple was introduced to Europe in the 16th century.
The pouch format is convenient for long‑term storage and transport without the need for glass jars.
Pineapple is widely used in Asian and Caribbean cuisines in marinades, sauces, and desserts.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: Bromelain helps break down proteins, improving digestion and reducing inflammation.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal heart function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned pineapple contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Supports digestive health
items.content: The fiber in pineapple promotes regular bowel movements and gut health.

items.title: Pineapple allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pineapple, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although packed in its own juice, the product still contains natural sugars; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Bromelain and medication
items.content: Bromelain can enhance the effect of anticoagulants; consult a doctor if you are taking such medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pineapple juice pack can be eaten as a snack, added to fruit salads, yogurts, smoothies, desserts, or used in sauces and marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the pouch in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep it refrigerated in a sealed container and consume within 3–4 days.

pizza-extra-cheese-thick-crust.title: Pizza with Extra Cheese, Thick Crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with extra cheese and a thick crust is a classic Italian dish made from leavened dough, topped with tomato sauce, a generous layer of mozzarella and an additional cheese (often cheddar or parmesan). The crust is dense yet soft, while the cheese forms a golden, stretchy layer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original pizza originated in Naples in the 18th‑19th centuries, while thick‑crust styles are popular in the American “deep‑dish” tradition.
Cheese boosts calcium and protein content but also raises the calorie count.
Thick‑crust dough often contains more oil, giving the crust a crispier texture.
In the United States, extra‑cheese pizza ranks among the top‑10 most ordered items in chain restaurants.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Cheese provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium for bones
items.content: Mozzarella and cheddar are rich in calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough supplies B1, B2, and B3 vitamins that aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Cooked tomatoes increase lycopene availability, which may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour in the dough adds fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The abundance of cheese and dough makes the pizza energy‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheeses contain saturated fats that can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Individuals sensitive to lactose may experience discomfort after eating.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and sauce often contain a lot of salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into bite‑size slices. Fresh toppings such as vegetables, basil, or a drizzle of olive oil can add balance and freshness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore a crispy crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard plain pretzels are a classic dry snack made from wheat flour, water, yeast and a pinch of salt. They have a crunchy crust and a faintly sweet, baked flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hard pretzels originated in medieval Europe and were a staple for sailors because they kept well on long voyages.
The traditional twisted shape is said to represent crossed arms in prayer.
In the 19th century the first large‑scale pretzel factories opened in the United States.
Hard pretzels are often used as a base for appetizers, such as cheese dips.
In some countries they are called “Brezel” or “Bretzel.”

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pretzels provide starch that offers lasting satiety.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Wheat flour supplies a modest amount of iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, hard pretzels contain virtually no fat when baked without added oil.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough contributes small amounts of thiamine, niacin and folate.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The simple composition and lack of heavy additives make them a light snack.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Pretzels can trigger reactions in people with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of their carbohydrate content, they can raise blood sugar quickly.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Even unsalted versions may contain trace amounts of sodium from processing.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: The hard texture can be a choking risk for young children or individuals with swallowing difficulties.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hard pretzels are convenient as a stand‑alone snack, broken into pieces for salads, soups, or as a crunchy base for cheese sauces. They can also be softened by soaking in milk or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Sugar‑free whipped topping is a light, creamy foam made from vegetable oils, stabilizers and non‑caloric sweeteners, containing no added sugar. It is designed for creating airy desserts, drinks and cake decorations while keeping carbohydrate content low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Its texture mimics traditional whipped cream but is dairy‑free.
Sweeteners are usually based on stevia or erythritol, making it suitable for keto and diabetic recipes.
The product is a common ingredient in low‑carb and sugar‑free baking.
Compared with regular cream, the added stabilizers give it a longer shelf life.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Absence of sugar helps maintain stable blood glucose levels, important for diabetics and low‑carb diets.

items.title: Source of plant fats
items.content: Contains vegetable oils that provide monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with lactose intolerance as it contains no dairy ingredients.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to soy or sunflower oil used in the formulation.

items.title: Sweetener sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of stevia or erythritol can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive persons.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Whip the sugar‑free topping until fluffy and use it as a topping for berries, cakes, coffee, cocktails and ice cream. It can also be folded into low‑carb desserts as a substitute for traditional whipped cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 2 °C‑6 °C. Once opened, consume within 7‑10 days. Discard if any off‑odor or discoloration appears.
